section_1.title: Intuitive Hook: The Observer's Perspective
section_1.content: Introduce the concept that coordinates are relative to an observer (the basis). Use a 'Robot Delivery' analogy: The robot needs to find a box. If we change the 'grid' the robot uses to see the world, the coordinate numbers change, but the physical location remains identical.
section_1.example: A robot at coordinate (2, 3) in Basis A. If we rotate the grid to Basis B, the robot is still at the same spot, but now reads as (1, 4). The 'where' is constant; the 'description' changes.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Review: Basis as Building Blocks
section_2.content: Briefly define a basis as a set of linearly independent vectors that span the space. Use a visual representation of the Standard Basis (i, j) vs. a Non-Standard Basis (u, v) represented by vectors pointing in different directions.
section_2.example: Standard Basis vectors are like the cardinal directions (North, East). A new basis is like using (Northeast, Northwest) to describe the same field.

section_3.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (The 'Translator')
section_3.content: Explain that moving from Basis B to Basis A requires a matrix P, where the columns are the Basis B vectors expressed in terms of Basis A coordinates. Visualize this as a 'transformation bridge' connecting two different grid overlays on the same 2D plane.
section_3.example: To convert coordinates [v]_B to [v]_A, compute [v]_A = P * [v]_B. If Basis B is { (1,1), (0,1) }, the matrix P = [[1, 0], [1, 1]].

section_4.title: Visualizing the Inverse
section_4.content: Discuss how to go back. If P takes us from B to A, P-inverse takes us from A to B. Show an animation where the coordinate grid 'stretches' and 'shears' to match the new basis.
section_4.example: If the robot reports its position in local grid coordinates (Basis B), we multiply by P-inverse to get its position on our global map (Standard Basis A).

section_5.title: Summary and Conclusion
section_5.content: Recap: Change of basis is a change of language, not a change of reality. Emphasize that finding the 'right' basis can simplify complex physics/engineering problems (e.g., diagonalizing matrices).
section_5.example: Final shot: A complex vector spinning in space; changing the basis allows us to view the rotation as a simple projection on one axis—making the math 10x easier.

section_1.title: Intuitive Hook: The Observer's Perspective
lecture_lines: Coordinates are relative to an observer.
A robot finds a box's location.
Changing the grid alters the description.
Physical location remains constant.
Language changes, reality stays the same.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Review: Basis as Building Blocks
lecture_lines: A basis is our building block.
Vectors must be linearly independent.
Standard basis uses cardinal directions.

section_3.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (The 'Translator')
lecture_lines: Need a translator between bases.
Columns are the new basis vectors.
Matrix P connects different grid overlays.
Convert [v]_B to [v]_A.
Compute [v]_A equals P times [v]_B.
animations: Place basis vectors b1, b2 into matrix columns (color #00FFFF).
Show the matrix multiplying coordinate vector [c1, c2].
Reveal the output as the original vector in standard basis.

Label this process as 'Change of Basis' [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/translator.svg].

section_4.title: Visualizing the Inverse
lecture_lines: How do we reverse the translation?
P-inverse takes us back to A.
Grid stretches and shears together.
animations: Show the Change of Basis matrix (color #00FFFF) overlaid on the [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/grid.svg].

section_5.title: Summary and Conclusion
lecture_lines: Change of basis is just language.
Simplifies complex physics and engineering.
Choosing the right basis helps.
